question: In the mid-1950s Americans made about 20 million copies a year. By 1966, with Xerox machines in offices, roughly how many?
answer: About 14 billion, by the estimates Brooks reports: 700 times as many. Before Xerox, copies meant carbon paper or fussy machines that made damp copies on special paper. Xerox’s dry copies on plain paper turned the urge into a mania. From 1939 to 1944 more than twenty companies had turned the inventor, Chester Carlson, down.
move: Demand for a hard thing says little about demand once it is easy.
trap: ‘About 200 million’: a tenfold boom already feels enormous.
simply: When notes had to be copied out by hand, people copied a page or two. Give everyone a copier and they copy everything, even things nobody would have bothered with before.
why: It is a warning for anyone sizing a market from today’s habits: making something cheap and effortless can create demand that no survey of current users would show.
